name: WojciechMula/toys avx512-string (AVX512F strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp)
baseline: libc strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp via <cstring> (labelled 'std' in the harness; libc version not stated)
workload: strlen/strchr/strrchr/strcmp over 10 kB strings on a Knights Landing CPU, AVX512F kernels (SWAR tricks since AVX512F has no byte ops) versus the stdlib routine.
tradeoffs: Requires AVX512F (Xeon Phi KNL, Skylake-X and later). The strlen kernel uses unaligned 64-byte loads that can read past the terminator and across a page boundary, so it is only safe on padded buffers (the harness pads by 64 bytes). Only four functions (strlen, strchr, strrchr, strcmp); no memcpy/memchr.
caveats: Author says the tests 'aren't very good' and do not cover a range of string lengths (single 10 kB size, zero byte moved through a '?' filled buffer, 5 iterations). Measured on one old CPU with GCC 5.4.3; the glibc version and which of its ifunc variants ran on KNL are not stated, so the baseline may be a weak SSE2 path. Date shown is the last commit touching avx512-string; the toys repo itself was last pushed 2026-04-08. An SSE2 version of the same four functions lives in a separate repo (WojciechMula/sse2string) whose README gives no numbers.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B listed WojciechMula/toys; its avx512-string subdirectory README holds the table

compiler_and_flags: cc (version not stated) with -Wall -ggdb3 -fPIC -fpic -O3; NASM -felf64 (from Makefile)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY 2.5 GHz (hypervisor VM) and AMD A8-6410 APU 2 GHz; AVX-512 row 'CPU is not supported' on the AMD machine
name: memcpy_benchmark (memcpy_avx256 and memcpy_movsb in NASM)
baseline: glibc memcpy as linked by the system cc (version not stated)
workload: One 128 MiB memcpy from a freshly malloc'd and memset source into a freshly malloc'd destination, repeated 10 times and timed with gettimeofday; compares libc memcpy, AVX2 loop, AVX-512 loop and rep movsb.
claimed_speedup: result.txt Avg seconds: Xeon Platinum 8269CY libc 0.3853, AVX 0.2987, AVX-512 0.3150, rep movsb 0.3333 (AVX about 1.29x vs libc, derived from page data); AMD A8-6410 libc 0.6221, AVX 0.4967, rep movsb 0.4970 (about 1.25x, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Single-size, large-buffer routines only (x86-64 Linux, NASM). The AVX/AVX-512 variants need the matching CPU features; rep movsb needs ERMS for good behaviour. Public-domain dedication, no patent grant. No handling shown for small or overlapping copies (memcpy only).
caveats: Only one 128 MiB size is measured, so small-copy behaviour (where glibc is strongest) is not covered. The timed region includes first-touch page faults on the freshly malloc'd destination, which dilutes and may distort the ratios. The loop runs 11 iterations but divides the total by 10 for 'Avg' (same bias for every variant). Compiler and glibc versions are not recorded. Gains of 25-29% on large copies are plausible non-temporal and wide-store effects, not a general memcpy win.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/memcpy listed ammarfaizi2/memcpy_benchmark ('Benchmark to show which is the fastest memcpy')

name: FastMemcpy
baseline: memcpy from the toolchain C runtime (gcc 4.9 or MSVC 2012; platform and libc not stated)
workload: Copy of 32 B to 8 MiB buffers (aligned and unaligned source/destination combinations, many repetitions) plus a random-size access run, memcpy_fast versus memcpy, SSE2 or AVX builds.
claimed_speedup: README: '50% speedup in avg. vs traditional memcpy in msvc 2012 or gcc 4.9'. gcc 4.9 rows (memcpy_fast vs memcpy, ms): 32 B x16777216 aligned 81 vs 281; 512 B aligned 124 vs 242; 8192 B aligned 55 vs 70; 4 MiB aligned 263 vs 398; random access 487 vs 1000. Slower case: 1 MiB aligned 181 vs 165.
tradeoffs: Header-style C implementation: jump table for small sizes, SSE2/AVX vector copy for medium, prefetch plus non-temporal stores (movntdq) for huge sizes. README notes that the AMD block-prefetch article it cites only covers aligned huge copies and that other cases are left to the user. SSE2 or AVX build must match the target CPU.
caveats: CPU model is not stated, gcc 4.9 and MSVC 2012 are very old, and the baseline libc/OS is not identified, so the 3x small-copy wins may reflect an old, slow memcpy rather than a current glibc with ifunc dispatch. Numbers are single-run and there are no modern glibc/musl comparisons. The README's 'over 50% in average' is not backed by a computed figure, and the 1 MiB aligned row shows memcpy_fast losing.
found_via: Direct check of known fast-memcpy projects (github.com/skywind3000/FastMemcpy); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: memset_benchmark (high-performance memset and memcpy in assembly)
baseline: glibc memset/memcpy (measured via the PLT and called directly), musl, and folly
workload: memset and memcpy of 0-512 byte buffers at varying sizes and offsets, with a randomized-size benchmark (precomputed random sizes 0-256, nop-call overhead subtracted) and a hot-loop benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README: 'These implementations outperform the folly and glibc implementations.' Results exist only as chart images (docs/memset_bench.png, docs/memcpy_bench.png, docs/memset_r.png, docs/memcpy_r.png), with no numeric table in the text; reading the charts, the memset line is at or below libc and musl over most of 0-512 B, while the memcpy chart is closer and mixed at small sizes (not stated in text).
stars_or_usage: 344 stars; README says the memset implementation landed in Folly (folly/memset.S)
tradeoffs: Assembly with reference C versions, plus a correctness tester, benchmark tool, size histogram tool and an LD_PRELOAD/DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES proxy to swap in the routines. Tuned for small buffers and the size distribution of desktop programs (Chrome, Vim, Python); x86-64 focus. No LICENSE file in the repo, so the code cannot be copied as is.
caveats: CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated, and the results are chart images only, so no number could be quoted. No licence file (usability reference), although the memset part reportedly went into Folly under that project's licence. The glibc 'direct' versus 'PLT' columns show how much of the gap is call indirection, not copy speed.

name: LibC-String-Optimisations (XEOS x86 and x86-64 string functions)
baseline: OS X 10.9 libc strlen, memset, memchr, memcpy, strcat (the README notes it is also heavily optimised); not glibc or musl
workload: 10,000,000 calls per function: strlen on 1000 chars, memset 4096 B, memchr 1000 B searching last char, memcpy 4096 B (aligned and misaligned), strcat on 1000 chars; 32-bit and 64-bit builds.
claimed_speedup: 64-bit: strlen 0.527532 s vs 0.531318 s OS X; memset 0.778556 s vs 0.906685 s; memchr 0.476380 s vs 0.516240 s; memcpy 0.858043 s vs 0.928405 s; strcat misaligned 1.423539 s vs 3.920867 s. 32-bit memchr 0.532130 s vs 6.374186 s. Loses: misaligned memcpy 1.408296 s vs OS X 1.218205 s (64-bit).
tradeoffs: x86 and x86-64 assembly only; SSE2 versions used when the CPU supports them, slower fallbacks otherwise. Developed for the XEOS operating system; README status badge says prototype. License is the XEOS Software License (README badge and text); no LICENSE file found at the repo root, and its terms were not verified, so treated as reference.
caveats: First-party numbers from the README only; the CPU, compiler and flags are not stated, and the baseline is the 2013-era OS X libc rather than glibc. Wins on most rows are 1-15%, the 12x memchr gain is against OS X's 32-bit memchr, and XEOS loses on misaligned memcpy. The strlen margin is under 1% (0.527532 s vs 0.531318 s).
found_via: WebSearch 'Show HN faster memcpy memset strlen than glibc ... assembly benchmark github' surfaced macmade/LibC-String-Optimisations; README opened via WebFetch and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: rt_memcpy_cm (Cortex-M assembly memcpy using LDMIA/STMIA)
baseline: RT-Thread rt_memcpy and the Keil C library memcpy (C library version not stated; baseline_in_list false because it is not glibc or musl)
workload: Copy 10,000 bytes, repeated 10,000 times, in a Keil build on a Cortex-M part (MCU not named).
claimed_speedup: README (Chinese): rt_memcpy 1261 ms, this assembly version 883 ms, C library memcpy 906 ms (about 1.43x vs rt_memcpy and about 1.03x vs the C library, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Cortex-M3/M4/M7 only; ports for Keil, GCC and IAR. Uses LDMIA/STMIA multi-register transfers (README: the gain is from those instructions, not from assembly itself) and handles addresses that are not 4-byte aligned. README says the assembly comes from Silicon Labs' uC/OS codebase.
caveats: The win over the C library memcpy is only about 2.5% (883 ms vs 906 ms); the headline gain is against RT-Thread's own rt_memcpy. Single test size, MCU and clock not stated, compiler flags unknown.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/memcpy listed mysterywolf/rt_memcpy_cm ('Assembly-optimized rt_memcpy for Cortex-M')

name: strstr.c (Ron Charlton)
baseline: C standard library strstr (compiler library strstr is row 0 of the 18 competitors in Competitors/strstrFunctions.c; library and version not stated)
workload: Finding English words in English text with a 15-line strchr-style strstr, compared with 18 other strstr implementations (BSD, GNU coreutils 5.3.0, Plauger, Moore, Visual C, compiler libraries).
claimed_speedup: README: 'tied for speed with its nearest competitor among 18 diverse strstr implementations' when finding English words in English text; 'Its other competitors are between 10.5% and 348% slower.' The README also says it 'is faster in many cases' than the C Standard Library's strstr.
tradeoffs: Plain C, no SIMD or table setup; 15 executable lines, public domain (CC0, no patent grant). Its inner loop is an unrolled strchr-like scan, so it relies on nothing platform specific.
caveats: Repo contains the competitor implementations but no timing harness, CPU model, compiler or flags, so the result is not reproducible from the repo. The competitors file header itself says that when the first pattern character is rare, versions that call the library's SIMD strchr (strstr7, 8, 15, 16) are about 6.5 times faster than strstr1/strstr20, so the claim holds only for the English-text workload and may lose to a modern libc strstr. The nearest competitor is a GPL implementation (GNU coreutils 5.3.0), so the speed tie is with old GNU code, not current glibc two-way strstr.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/strstr listed charltoncr/strstr.c ('Faster standard C library string search')

name: wasi-libc SIMD string routines (Wasm SIMD128 strlen, memchr, memcmp, strchr and others)

workload: Wasm SIMD128 reimplementations of string.h routines run under wazero (and spot checks on wasmtime) versus the existing musl implementation, long strings (a 4 MB string was asked about in the thread) and 10-byte strings.
claimed_speedup: Issue 580 (author's May 9 2025 table, rough, wazero only): memchr 4.3x, memcmp 10.0x, strlen 4.9x, strchr 4.2x, strrchr 9.9x, strcmp 12.8x, strncmp 16.3x, strspn 9.1x, strcspn 9.7x, strstr 5.6x, geomean 7.8x. Original post: some functions 'around 4x faster' with SIMD128, others 'can make them 16x faster'. For 10-byte strings on wasmtime on amd64 the improvement 'is still around 2x'.
license: Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, Apache-2.0 and MIT (multi-licensed); musl parts MIT
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; wasi-libc is the C library of wasi-sdk (changelog line seen only in a WebSearch snippet)

Per the issue timeline, strlen (PR 586) and memchr (PR 592) are confirmed merged, and strchrnul, memrchr, memcmp and str(c)spn commits were listed; strstr, strncmp and some other table rows may exist only in the author's go-sqlite3 libc and not upstream.
caveats: The table is the contributor's own rough wazero run (not wasmtime or a browser), hardware not named, and the baseline is the previous wasm code rather than a native libc; PR 592 says on wasmtime (Xeon W-2135) memchr was 'hard to measure' and 'close enough' to the old one, so wins depend on the runtime. Wazero has a weak compiler, which can exaggerate SIMD gains. Per-function table is for the author's version, which may be wider than what was merged upstream. name: WebAssembly memory.copy (bulk-memory-operations proposal)
baseline: Emscripten-generated wasm memcpy loop (aligned i32.load/i32.store) used in the Unity demo, plus manually unrolled i32 and i64 load/store loop variants
workload: Each row copies 1 GiB in total with a V8 prototype where memcpy/memmove exports are replaced by memory.copy, versus the wasm loops; copy sizes 32 B to 1 MiB within a 1 MiB working set.
claimed_speedup: At 128 KiB: memory.copy 29.728 Gib/s vs i64 load/store x4 10.032, i64 x2 7.934, i32 x2 3.975, plain i32 loop 2.782 Gib/s. At 1.0 KiB: 17.902 vs 7.010, 6.112, 3.568, 2.614 Gib/s. Loses at 32 B: intrinsic 1.382 vs i64 x4 1.565 Gib/s. At 1 MiB: 11.760 vs 10.091 Gib/s.
tradeoffs: A proposal text plus a hacked V8 prototype, not a library. The repo's LICENSE file points to per-directory licences (document/ under the W3C Software and Document Notice and License). The instruction itself is a runtime feature, so the benefit applies only to engines that call native MemMove for memory.copy.
caveats: Baseline is a 2018-era Emscripten wasm loop, not a native libc or musl memcpy; engine, V8 version and CPU model are not given, and the benchmark and loop sources are in gists that were not opened. Prototype benchmark by one author, so first-party. The repo is archived and does not itself state whether the proposal was merged into the standard.
found_via: Directed check of the WebAssembly bulk-memory proposal after the wasi-libc search (wasm memcpy baseline); Overview.md opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2026 with WDK and /std:c++20 (README prerequisites); optimisation flags and compiler version for the benchmarks not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-1165G7 (bare-metal Windows 11, AVX-512BW) and Intel Core i7-8086K (VMware guest Windows 11, AVX2 only)
name: KmStrSearch (Windows kernel UTF-8 and UTF-16 substring search)
baseline: Windows kernel CRT strstr and wcsstr (MSVC runtime; not glibc or musl)
workload: Single match near the end of a buffer (40 B to 1 MB for 8-bit, 80 B to 2 MB for 16-bit) and a worst-case mismatched dense text (repetitive partial matches), run through a multi-threaded kernel driver harness; hybrid Boyer-Moore-Horspool with SWAR, AVX2 and AVX-512BW engines versus CRT.
claimed_speedup: i7-1165G7, 8-bit, GB/s (CRT baseline vs Smart Auto): 10 KB 22.38 vs 45.71, 1 MB 22.66 vs 85.93; 16-bit 20 KB 26.67 vs 68.43. Worse on small buffers: 40 B 3.61 vs 1.95, 256 B 15.03 vs 4.88. README: on mismatched dense text CRT collapses to 0.21-0.37 GB/s while the hybrid delivers 49-81 GB/s, 'up to 385x faster'.
tradeoffs: Windows kernel-mode (WDK driver) code: routes small buffers to a SWAR path to avoid the KeSaveExtendedProcessorState cost of entering vector mode, and uses AVX2/AVX-512BW or ARM64 NEON for larger buffers. Uses 8 KB (UTF-16) skip tables allocated from paged pool. Not a user-mode library; the README says user-mode (TestUm) timings cannot be trusted.
caveats: Very new, single-author exploration ('not strictly benchmark-driven during its design'); no repetition counts or variance reported, compiler flags not stated, and throughput comes from a multi-threaded harness built to saturate the memory bus, so GB/s figures are aggregate and not per-call latency. The CRT baseline measures only 1.35-1.67 GB/s on the VMware guest for small to large buffers and to 0.21-0.37 GB/s on dense mismatches, which reflects that CRT implementation, not glibc/musl (glibc uses a two-way algorithm for long needles). Loses to CRT on tiny and small buffers. Kernel driver telemetry only; no independent reproduction.
